video_title: The Next Frontier of AI Is Spatial Intelligence | Fei-Fei Li on a16z
gist: Fei-Fei Li and the co-founder of robotics-simulation startup Scenix explain World Labs' acquisition of Scenix and lay out a 'real-to-sim-to-real' thesis: robotics is bottlenecked on training data and, more acutely, on evaluation, and geometrically consistent generated 3D worlds (World Labs' Marble base model) — not video-only prediction models — are the scalable substitute. Both push back on humanoid timelines, arguing near-term value sits in semi-structured environments like warehouses, and that World Labs will sell model-agnostic, embodiment-agnostic simulation infrastructure rather than build robots itself.

themes.theme: World Labs' Spatial Intelligence Thesis & the Scenix Deal

insights.claim: World Labs, a two-year-old frontier model lab, defines its category as 'spatial intelligence' — AI that can generate, understand, reason with and interact with physical or virtual spaces — with large world models as the means to that end.
insights.speaker: Fei-Fei Li
insights.so_what: Establishes a frontier-lab category competing for the same capital and talent as LLM labs but on 3D world modeling; watch whether 'spatial intelligence' hardens into an investable sector label distinct from video generation.
insights.quote: we are building the next frontier of AI which is what we call spatial intelligence

insights.claim: Marble is World Labs' base model, publicly released around November–December of the prior winter, which converts a text prompt or one-to-few images into a geometrically consistent 3D world represented as gaussian splats or mesh.
insights.speaker: Fei-Fei Li
insights.so_what: Marble is the shippable, revenue-touching asset under the spatial-intelligence narrative, and its output format — explicit 3D geometry rather than frames — is the technical fork versus video-model competitors.

insights.claim: The Scenix acquisition originated as inbound product-led demand rather than a relationship deal: Scenix signed up as a Marble customer and Fei-Fei Li only later realized the account belonged to her former Stanford postdoc, while World Labs was separately fielding robotics inbound for Marble it could not serve.
insights.speaker: Fei-Fei Li
insights.so_what: Bottom-up adoption by sophisticated robotics teams, plus unserved inbound demand, is stronger evidence of real product-market fit than a top-down strategic acquisition narrative.
insights.quote: They came into World Wars as a customer.

insights.claim: World Labs is not ruling out shipping a robotics foundation model, framing the likely form as an omni-model that takes multimodal input and emits actions as an output modality.
insights.speaker: Fei-Fei Li
insights.so_what: If World Labs moves from world-simulation infrastructure into action-producing models, it becomes a direct competitor to the robotics-model companies it currently sells to — a channel-conflict risk worth tracking.
insights.quote: it's very likely going to involve the output of actions in addition to the state of the world and we're definitely not ruling this out

insights.claim: Treating action as a modality yields two distinct model types from one architecture: action-as-input is a forward simulator predicting how the environment changes, action-as-output is a policy model predicting the next action toward a goal — and such an omni-model can serve as a backbone for fine-tuning into specific robotic applications.
insights.speaker: guest, Scenix co-founder and Columbia professor
insights.so_what: A clean diligence lens for robotics-model startups: ask which direction of the action channel the model runs, and whether it can serve as a fine-tuning backbone for others.

themes.theme: Consistency Over Video: The Real-to-Sim-to-Real Bet

insights.claim: Video-only world prediction models fail robotics because they break object permanence — an object a robot pushes can simply vanish — which provides no usable learning signal, making consistency across space, time, viewpoints and interaction types a hard requirement.
insights.speaker: guest, Scenix co-founder and Columbia professor
insights.so_what: A concrete falsification test for the fashionable 'just use a video model' robotics pitch; diligence should probe object permanence under interaction, not just visual quality.
insights.quote: Imagine if a robot push an object forwards. The object just magically disappear which has been a problem of many of the existing like video prediction models.

insights.claim: The unique and irreplaceable role of simulation is counterfactual reasoning — playing out events that have not happened or cannot happen — which real-world data collection structurally cannot supply, mirroring how humans simulate internally before acting.
insights.speaker: Fei-Fei Li
insights.so_what: Reframes simulation from a cost-saving proxy for real data into a category of data that cannot be collected at all, which is the strongest argument that simulation spend is durable rather than transitional.
insights.quote: There's a very important role simulation plays that real world data doesn't play which is counterfactual reasoning

insights.claim: Waymo has officially stated it uses billions of hours of simulation and is more simulation-heavy than real-world-data-heavy, cited as the existence proof for sim-first robotics given that cars are the simplest kind of robot.
insights.speaker: Fei-Fei Li
insights.so_what: The only robotics business deployed at scale already runs sim-heavy — a direct analog argument that general robotics converges on the same data mix, favoring simulation-infrastructure vendors.
insights.quote: Whimo has officially said they use billions of hours of simulation

insights.claim: The rebuttal to Sergey Levine's objection that simulation always deviates from the physical world is that the two are not in conflict: the world model can be part physics and part learned, weighted toward physics early in the data flywheel for consistency and shifting toward learned modeling as real deployment and client data accumulate.
insights.speaker: guest, Scenix co-founder and Columbia professor
insights.so_what: Positions the simulation approach as absorbing rather than opposing the real-data camp; the checkable milestone is whether the physics-to-learning weighting actually shifts as customer data lands.

insights.claim: Simulators do not need to be photorealistic or physically exact — they need to capture the essential structure of the problem plus heavy randomization, evidenced by quadrupeds and bipeds that walk on snow and through bushes despite no simulator precisely modeling snow or bushes.
insights.speaker: guest, Scenix co-founder and Columbia professor
insights.so_what: Lowers the fidelity, compute and capex bar for commercially useful simulation, which is bullish for simulation-vendor unit economics versus assumptions that photorealistic fidelity is a prerequisite.

themes.theme: Evaluation as the Overlooked Robotics Bottleneck

insights.claim: Evaluation, not training, is the underappreciated robotics bottleneck: the industry's real criterion is wall-clock time to distinguish a 90%-success checkpoint from a 92% one, and doing that physically makes robotics iteration multiple orders of magnitude slower than language-model iteration.
insights.speaker: guest, Scenix co-founder and Columbia professor
insights.so_what: Iteration velocity rather than model architecture may be the real moat in robotics — a company that compresses evaluation wall-clock time compounds faster than one with a better starting model.
insights.quote: the iteration speeds is multiple orders of magnitude slower than iterations of those language models

insights.claim: Scenix's commercial wedge is a demonstrated alignment claim documented in its blog post — a checkpoint that performs better in their simulation is highly likely to perform better in the real environment — which is what gives customers confidence to substitute simulated evaluation for physical evaluation.
insights.speaker: guest, Scenix co-founder and Columbia professor
insights.so_what: Rank-order correlation between simulation and reality is the single metric that makes or breaks this business model, and is the sharpest diligence question to press on any sim-eval vendor.
insights.quote: If a checkpoint is working better in the simulation is also highly likely to also work better in the real environments

insights.claim: Simulation delivers two separable commercial benefits: reliability, via systematic randomization of lighting, friction, geometry, object types and physical parameters to guarantee state-space coverage, and efficiency, which real-world data collection cannot address at all.
insights.speaker: guest, Scenix co-founder and Columbia professor
insights.so_what: Two distinct buying triggers mean two separable product lines and pricing arguments, useful for sizing addressable spend beyond the generic 'robotics needs more data' claim.

insights.claim: Teleoperation collects robot training data more slowly than a human performing the task, yet industrial customers demand faster-than-human speeds, and a robot cannot simply be driven faster because gravity does not change — whereas simulation can systematically speed up behaviors while accounting for the altered dynamics.
insights.speaker: guest, Scenix co-founder and Columbia professor
insights.so_what: A hard physical argument that teleoperation-data businesses hit a ceiling on the dimension customers most care about — throughput — which is bearish for teleop-only data moats.
insights.quote: So for the robot to like move faster, it's not as simple as just drive the robot faster because the gravity doesn't change.

insights.claim: Robotics faces a stricter reliability bar than language models because LLM output still passes through a human who reads it before consequential actions like booking flights or hotels, whereas robot policies must work reliably out of the box in the physical environment.
insights.speaker: guest, Scenix co-founder and Columbia professor
insights.so_what: Explains why robotics cannot ride the 'good enough with a human in the loop' adoption curve that made LLM products deployable early, and why evaluation infrastructure is a prerequisite rather than a nice-to-have.
insights.quote: for robotic models out of the box the robots has to work reliably in the real environment

themes.theme: Model- and Embodiment-Agnostic Infrastructure, Not Robots

insights.claim: World Labs and Scenix are explicitly not building robots or hardware — they are building the environment infrastructure into which another company places its robot brain to learn and be evaluated.
insights.speaker: guest, Scenix co-founder and Columbia professor
insights.so_what: Positions the company as an arms dealer to the robotics sector rather than a competitor to it — a higher-margin, lower-capex profile than humanoid hardware plays.

insights.claim: The platform is deliberately embodiment-agnostic across single arms, fixed arms, mobile manipulators, bipeds, grippers and more elaborate end effectors, and model-agnostic — its generated data can train models from scratch or post-train existing vision-language-action or world-action models.
insights.speaker: guest, Scenix co-founder and Columbia professor
insights.so_what: Agnosticism means the business wins regardless of which embodiment or model architecture converges — a form-factor-neutral way to get robotics exposure without picking the winner.
insights.quote: So our platform right now is just naturally embodiment agnostic.

insights.claim: The offering is unbundled by pipeline stage — some customers buy only the real-to-sim step to digitize a task and evaluate their systems, others buy the full real-to-sim-to-real pipeline to run policies on their own hardware — and current customers are already close to deployment with tens to hundreds of instances of the same automation task.
insights.speaker: guest, Scenix co-founder and Columbia professor
insights.so_what: A two-tier structure implies a low-friction land motion (evaluation only) with natural expansion into full policy training, and deployment-stage buyers with repeat volume signal better revenue quality than research pilots.

insights.claim: The stated two-year success case is validated customers in a small number of important vertical use cases that become lighthouse references to scale the business — a deliberately narrow land-and-expand rather than a horizontal platform launch.
insights.speaker: Fei-Fei Li
insights.so_what: Sets a concrete, checkable two-year milestone for judging execution — named vertical logos, not model benchmarks.

insights.claim: World Labs is deliberately not rushing post-merger integration of Scenix's codebase, teams, tech stack or customers, integrating first only on the simulation and action-conditioned base model surfaces while Scenix consumes Marble as an internal customer.
insights.speaker: Fei-Fei Li
insights.so_what: Preserving Scenix's contained stack and customer base lowers integration risk and keeps its revenue line intact — a positive execution signal versus acquisitions that dissolve the acquired product.
insights.quote: we're not rushing to blend the team as like a full salad bowl

insights.claim: Predictions around humanoids have been too aggressive and rollouts will be more constrained, because robotic deployment has always progressed from fully structured environments like car-manufacturing factories, to semi-structured ones like Amazon warehouses, restaurants and hotels, before reaching unstructured homes.
insights.speaker: guest, Scenix co-founder and Columbia professor
insights.so_what: A staged-adoption framework arguing near-term robotics revenue concentrates in semi-structured commercial settings — bearish for consumer humanoid timelines, bullish for warehouse and hospitality automation exposure.

insights.claim: Fei-Fei Li argues the humanoid form factor is a category error for business purposes: evolution optimized the human body for general survival in unstructured environments, so it is best at nothing in particular, making a general body in an unstructured environment the hardest problem and not necessarily the right way to solve it.
insights.speaker: Fei-Fei Li
insights.so_what: A first-principles argument for specialized morphologies over humanoids that cuts against the dominant humanoid capital narrative and favors task-specific embodiment plays.
insights.quote: It's not necessarily even the right way to solve the problem.

insights.claim: A public survey run with Fei-Fei Li collected roughly a thousand tasks people want robots to do for them and found one-third were about cleaning, indicating consumer demand concentrates on dull and dirty chores rather than general-purpose assistance.
insights.speaker: guest, Scenix co-founder and Columbia professor
insights.so_what: Hard demand data suggesting the household robotics TAM is heavily weighted toward cleaning, which bears on whether general humanoids or specialized cleaning machines capture consumer spend.
insights.quote: Among the thousand tasks we collected, onethird of the tasks are about clean.

insights.claim: Robots matching human power efficiency on menial minimum-wage-type tasks will take a very long time, because a working robot is always a full system spanning hardware, software, brain and details down to the friction coefficient of its fingers — so no single model breakthrough collapses the timeline.
insights.speaker: guest, Scenix co-founder and Columbia professor
insights.so_what: Directly contradicts near-term labor-replacement models used to justify humanoid valuations; the systems argument implies incremental, iteration-bound progress rather than a step change.
insights.quote: I think it's going to take a very long time.

insights.claim: The economic case for LLMs works because human brains are inefficient at producing prose and code, which LLMs do roughly ten thousand times faster and much cheaper, but human brains and bodies are highly efficient at 3D navigation and manipulation, so the same economic argument does not transfer to robotics.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: A clean economic screen for physical-AI investments: the incumbent human is a far tougher cost benchmark in robotics than in knowledge work, compressing achievable margins.

insights.claim: The human brain runs on 30 watts, a level even LLMs do not approach, though performance-per-power may already be close in narrow tasks like image generation or software engineering — and is nowhere close in robotics.
insights.speaker: Fei-Fei Li
insights.so_what: Quantifies the energy gap gating embodied-AI economics and implies efficiency progress in narrow digital tasks does not read through to robotics.

insights.claim: Fei-Fei Li frames calibrated expectation-setting as the scarcest skill in the current AI cycle, calling measured optimism the hardest thing in today's AI, while her co-guest notes robot-learning state of the art has consistently moved faster than he expected since his PhD.
insights.speaker: Fei-Fei Li
insights.so_what: A barbell view — fast capability progress, slow economic parity — argues for capital in tooling and infrastructure that compounds with progress rather than end-applications priced on parity timelines.
insights.quote: the hardest thing in today's AI is to have the right measured optimism
